_Story by Blake Burdge. Published in collaboration with[Belly of the
Beast](https://substack.com/@bellyofthebeastcuba)._

In September, a rare public opinion poll backed by two major U.S. universities
suggested that Cubans overwhelmingly blame their own government for the
country's economic crisis and do not oppose a U.S. military intervention.

The results appeared to vindicate the Trump administration's hard-line
policies toward the island.

But a close look at the survey, which has been
[promoted](https://www.vanderbilt.edu/cgd/press/pbs-news-hour-cites-
americasbarometer-data-in-interview-with-cuban-official/) as "the first-ever
nationally representative study" of Cuba and has been cited by [PBS
NewsHour](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FzYJ9acmjIQ&vl=en),
[Americas](https://www.americasquarterly.org/article/cubas-debate-is-missing-
what-cubans-want/) _[](https://www.americasquarterly.org/article/cubas-debate-
is-missing-what-cubans-
want/)_[Quarterly](https://www.americasquarterly.org/article/cubas-debate-is-
missing-what-cubans-want/) and
[Foreign](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/cuba/cubas-point-no-return)
_[](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/cuba/cubas-point-no-
return)_[Affairs](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/cuba/cubas-point-no-return),
reveals a stark disconnect between how the poll was presented and what its
findings actually show.

Media coverage also failed to examine the millions of dollars in U.S.
government funding received by the organizations connected to the poll--
including for programs aimed at influencing the very public opinion the poll
sought to measure.

##### In this video, Belly of the Beast asked Cubans in the streets of Havana
whether they would support a U.S. military intervention.

## The Money Behind the Poll

The poll was overseen by Vanderbilt University's Latin American Public Opinion
Project Lab (LAPOP), which [describes](https://cdn.vanderbilt.edu/vu-wpfsx/wp-
content/uploads/sites/157/2026/11/2026_Pulse-of-Democracy_20261105.pdf) its
flagship survey, AmericasBarometer, as "the leading source of comparative
public opinion data on democracy and governance across the Americas" since
2004.

Data from AmericasBarometer frequently appears in[ State Department
reports](https://2021-2025.state.gov/reports/2023-report-on-international-
religious-freedom/ecuador/?safe=1),[ academic
research](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11300036/), and the World
Bank's "[governance
indicators](https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/worldwide-governance-
indicators/documentation)."

Every two or three years, AmericasBarometer publishes a region-wide report
called Pulse of Democracy. This year's report features polls from 21
countries, including, for the first time, Cuba.

For the Cuba poll, LAPOP contracted a company called CubaData
([incorporated](https://search.sunbiz.org/Inquiry/CorporationSearch/GetDocument?aggregateId=flal-l18000125347-8bc5621d-382a-4a38-9440-5fc8e890b782&transactionId=l18000125347-60fc5e05-5ad2-4fff-8b0a-9c8e78ac856e&formatType=PDF)
in Titusville, Florida, as Cuba Data LLC) that specializes in conducting
digital surveys on the island via cell phone.

CubaData is co-owned by Pablo Diaz Espi, a Cuban exile who [left the island
for Germany](https://www.ned.org/events/the-legacy-of-laura-pollan-the-
struggle-for-democracy-and-human-rights-in-cuba/) shortly after the fall of
the Berlin Wall. Diaz Espi [has lived between Berlin
and](https://miamibookfair.com/mbf-author/pablo-diaz-espi/) Spain, where he is
the founder of a Madrid-based news outlet called Diario de Cuba whose agenda
is to "[go for the jugular of
Castroism](https://havanatimes.org/interviews/interview-with-diario-de-cuba-
editor-pablo-diaz/)."

Both Diario de Cuba and CubaData have been the beneficiaries of U.S.
government funding.

Between 2013 and 2021 _,_ Diario de Cuba received grants totaling at least
$2.3 million from the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), according to
figures published in annual reports, academic studies, and news articles. NED
describes itself as a non-governmental organization that "promotes democracy"
around the world, but it receives its entire budget from Congress and has
assumed many of the CIA's former activities, funding political parties,
unions, media outlets, and other civil society organizations to advance U.S.
foreign policy objectives.

"A lot of what we do today was done covertly 25 years ago by the CIA," Allen
Weinstein, a former NED president,[ told the Washington Post in
1991](https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/opinions/1991/09/22/innocence-
abroad-the-new-world-of-spyless-coups/92bb989a-de6e-4bb8-99b9-462c76b59a16/).

post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3f7a101d-a1fe-46df-8c29-a39aa7c704a1_1500x1340.png)The
National Endowment for Democracy awarded $2,387,601 in grants to Asociacion
Diario de Cuba between 2013 and 2021 according to NED grant figures for
[2013](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/2013-ned-
annualreportfullfinal/77930859),
[2014](https://web.archive.org/web/20150807063122/https://www.ned.org/region/latin-
america-and-caribbean/cuba-2014/),
[2015](https://web.archive.org/web/20171205202310/https://www.ned.org/region/latin-
america-and-caribbean/cuba-2015/),
[2016](https://web.archive.org/web/20171205180421/https://www.ned.org/region/latin-
america-and-caribbean/cuba-2016/),
[2017](https://web.archive.org/web/20180726073352/https://www.ned.org/region/latin-
america-and-caribbean/cuba-2017/),
[2018](https://web.archive.org/web/20220117173706/https://www.ned.org/region/latin-
america-and-caribbean/cuba-2018/),
[2019](https://web.archive.org/web/20210129185734/https://www.ned.org/region/latin-
america-and-caribbean/cuba-2019/),
[2020](https://web.archive.org/web/20210703143056id_/https://www.ned.org/region/latin-
america-and-caribbean/cuba-2020/) and
[2021](https://web.archive.org/web/20220218051854/https://www.ned.org/region/latin-
america-and-caribbean/cuba-2021/), as published in annual reports, academic
studies and media reports.

In 2026, NED is [disbursing $8.5 million in Cuba
grants](https://www.ned.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/July-2026-Active-Grant-
Listings_Final.pdf), including programs to "challenge the state's narrative by
exposing regime failures," expose the Cuban government's "malign influence in
Latin America," and disseminate research on dismantling Cuba's power
structures in a "post-authoritarian context."

Whether Diario de Cuba has continued to receive funding is difficult to
determine because NED no longer publicly identifies many grant recipients, a
policy it says is intended to protect them from government retaliation. Last
year, however, NED President Damon Wilson and board member Mel Martinez, a
former Republican senator from Florida, [praised reporting by NED
partners](https://www.miamiherald.com/opinion/op-ed/article305172656.html),
including Diario de Cuba, saying they "undermine the regime's legitimacy."

In addition to NED funding, Diario de Cuba has also received money from the
State Department. In September 2020, the U.S. Embassy in Havana awarded the
outlet a $12,960 contract for news-monitoring services,[ according to federal
procurement
records](https://www.usaspending.gov/search?hash=25a8a6fd8ee6a6d875a995eb70c65b16).
In 2022, the outlet received a $530,000 State Department grant "to strengthen
Cuban civil society and boost youth participation in advancing democratic
demands," [according to the federal grant database
HigherGov](https://www.highergov.com/grant/SAQMIP22GR0357/).

CubaData has also received funding from NED.

In 2021, the company was the beneficiary of a [$500,000 grant
awarded](https://web.archive.org/web/20220218051854/https://www.ned.org/region/latin-
america-and-caribbean/cuba-2021/) to the National Democratic Institute (NDI),
an organization affiliated with the Democratic Party that was established to
receive NED funding and carry out U.S.-funded democracy-promotion programs
abroad. NDI contracted CubaData to use polling data "to analyze Cubans' needs,
perceptions and beliefs about topics of public interest."

At the time, NDI's Cuba program was
[headed](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/biden-cuba-
policy/2021/06/27/dde275f6-d0f6-11eb-8014-2f3926ca24d9_story.htm) by Karla
Velasquez Figuera, a Venezuelan lawyer based in Mexico who served as an
intermediary between Cuban dissidents and the State Department, [according to
The Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/biden-
cuba-policy/2021/06/27/dde275f6-d0f6-11eb-8014-2f3926ca24d9_story.html). Cuban
state television [aired](https://www.granma.cu/pensar-en-qr/2021-05-03/el-
ahijado-la-madrina-y-la-mas-reciente-farsa-contra-cuba-03-05-2021-00-05-44)
intercepted telephone and text exchanges between Velasquez and dissidents,
portraying her as the "godmother" of the San Isidro Movement, a prominent
anti-government organization.

Velasquez also carried out
"[training](https://www.programacuba.com/cubacrisishumanitariacontinuada)"
activities at Diario de Cuba for Diaz Espi. The experience, [she
said](https://www.programacuba.com/cubacrisishumanitariacontinuada) in a
recent interview, led to her later being hired as "[project
director](https://cubadata.com/quienes-somos/)" for CubaData.

In a[ 2025 CubaData
report](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1QyOwJN2koo5Iwix4BLZDpIfAvA8v0lLc/view)
about "latent dissidence" in Cuba, Velasquez thanked NED and NDI for making it
possible to implement the study's data-collection methodology.

Velasquez did not respond to a request for comment about her work with NDI,
Diario de Cuba, and CubaData.

CubaData runs its polls through a mobile phone app called Apretaste, which is
owned by a software developer called Agora Cuba, a nonprofit organization
[incorporated](https://search.sunbiz.org/Inquiry/CorporationSearch/SearchResultDetail?inquirytype=EntityName&directionType=Initial&searchNameOrder=AGORACUBA%20N110000100260&aggregateId=domnp-n11000010026-a305d252-3d51-4915-81f3-b7ff9a0e5b5b&searchTerm=AGORA%20CUBA%20INC&listNameOrder=AGORACUBA%20N110000100260)
at the same Titusville, Florida address as CubaData. Agora Cuba's executive
director is Salvador "Salvi" Pascual, a Cuban-born technology entrepreneur
based in Florida who co-founded CubaData with Diaz Espi in 2018. Agora Cuba,
like Diario de Cuba and CubaData, has received U.S. government funding.

Between 2016 and 2021, NED's[ tax
records](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/521344831)
document more than $332,000 in grants to Agora Cuba, according to NED's grant
listings and tax filings. An NED grant of $44,252 listed for 2021 was
equivalent to more than 94 percent of Agora Cuba's reported revenue that year.

National Endowment for Democracy provided $332,198 in documented grants to
Agora Cuba between 2016 and 2021 according to NED Form 990 tax filings for
[2016,](https://web.archive.org/web/20171205180421/https://www.ned.org/region/latin-
america-and-caribbean/cuba-2016/)
[2017](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/521344831/201822279349301872/full),

and

LAPOP itself has also long relied on U.S. government funding. In October 2024,
Vanderbilt[ announced](https://as.vanderbilt.edu/news/2024/10/10/center-for-
global-democracy-awarded-12-5-million-from-usaid) a five-year, $12.5 million
USAID award to support the project and other surveys. USAID was reportedly
supplying[ about 70% of LAPOP's AmericasBarometer's
budget](https://www.ndsmcobserver.com/article/2025/10/tarbaujenbsk).

But that funding was cut off in 2025 when Elon Musk's Department of Government
Efficiency (DOGE) dismantled USAID.

Notre Dame's Kellogg Institute for International Studies stepped in to help
fund half of this year's AmericasBarometer budget, [according to the school's
campus newspaper The
Observer](https://www.ndsmcobserver.com/article/2025/10/tarbaujenbsk).
Vanderbilt University officials contacted by Belly of the Beast and Drop Site
did not respond to questions about how they funded the other half.

post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6aecb59c-c65c-41db-aeae-
da5089847ba0_2048x1280.png)U.S. government funding and institutional ties
among the organizations involved in the 2026 AmericasBarometer survey of Cuba.
Sources: NED grant records and tax filings, federal spending records, Florida
corporate records, LAPOP technical documentation, CubaData, Diario de Cuba,
and interviews conducted by Belly of the Beast.

## U.S.-Funded Apps

The U.S. government has long funded media and communications projects aimed at
bringing about regime change in Cuba.

Journalist Tracey Eaton[ documented](https://www.american.edu/centers/latin-
american-latino-studies/upload/eaton_dem-projects-in-cuba.pdf) more than $218
million in U.S. government disbursements for Cuba "democracy promotion" (also
known as "regime change") programs between 2001 and 2021. Roughly $25 million
went to media and information projects, of which NED managed $15.6 million.

Some programs have clearly stated their intentions. For example, a 2019 USAID
initiative [offered up to $2
million](https://apply07.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/287363)
for projects that would "dispel the myths about the successes of the Cuban
Revolution," including its education and healthcare systems.

Other programs were covert. One of the most notorious was ZunZuneo, a text-
message network modeled on Twitter that launched in Cuba in 2010 thanks to
$1.7 million in funding from USAID.

ZunZuneo's plan was to attract subscribers with sports, music, and weather
updates, and then introduce political content that could spark anti-government
protests, according to documents[ obtained by the Associated
Press](https://apnews.com/article/technology-cuba-united-states-
government-904a9a6a1bcd46cebfc14bea2ee30fdf?utm_source=copy&utm_medium=share)
in 2014.

More than 40,000 Cubans used the network without knowing the U.S. government
was behind it.

The revelations embarrassed USAID and led to Congress grilling its
administrator, Rajiv Shah. Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-Vt.), who chaired the
subcommittee overseeing the agency's funding, [called the
project](https://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Latest-News-Wires/2014/0408/Cuban-
Twitter-What-was-USAID-thinking) "dumb, dumb, dumb."

More than a decade later, the U.S. government is surreptitiously funding
another social media app aimed at Cubans.

Apretaste, the app CubaData uses to recruit and register its survey
respondents, bills itself as a free social network for Cubans, promising users
the freedom to express themselves "without fear of censorship." Its [app-store
listings](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/apretaste/id1488232603) name Agora
Cuba as its developer but make no mention of its NED funding.

Salvador Pascual, Agora Cuba's executive director,[ told
EFE](https://www.tvn-2.com/entretenimiento/tecnologia/software/miami-
aplicaciones-conectar-estadounidenses-cubanos_1_1618995.html) in a 2016
interview that the app would be used to conduct market research and polling
for U.S. companies. "We are the only ones who have this information about
Cuban people, who also want to socialize," he said.

The app has been used[ repeatedly to recruit people to participate in polls
conducted by CubaData](https://cubadata.com/encuestas/), which is [run by Diaz
Espi](https://cubadata.com/quienes-somos/). Those polls in turn are regularly
[publicized](https://diariodecuba.com/foro-ddc/1791457282_69285.html) in Diaz
Espi's Diario de Cuba.

Asked about the potential for bias in hiring a polling organization that is
both funded by the U.S. government and led by an outspoken exile known for his
anti-government activism, Jordan responded that LAPOP "adheres to rigorous
scientific standards to ensure that its research is non-partisan."

In a written response via email, Diaz Espi told Belly of the Beast and Drop
Site that Diario de Cuba did not participate in the LAPOP survey or share
staff, resources, or user databases with CubaData or Agora Cuba. He said he
did not participate in the survey's design, implementation, or analysis, and
that his own role was "exclusively institutional." He did not specify what
that meant.

He said NED and NDI supported separate, earlier research conducted by
CubaData, but did not finance LAPOP's Cuba poll.

Pascual did not respond to requests for comment.

## How Blame Became the Headline

The Cuba poll asked 73 questions, but one of them has dominated media coverage
of it: "Who is primarily responsible for the current crisis facing Cuba?"

Respondents could make only one choice.

Seventy-four percent chose the Cuban government. Sixteen percent chose the
U.S. government.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1Lz3!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6ab4e9a1-aa9d-440c-a6fc-536b32313f6a_878x256.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1Lz3!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6ab4e9a1-aa9d-440c-a6fc-536b32313f6a_878x256.jpeg)

Another question allowed respondents to assign blame to multiple actors. More
than 45% attributed the crisis to U.S. sanctions or policies, either entirely
or in part.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9YHv!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6c9a4adc-
ad14-4281-9562-27aa1f4db0e4_866x214.jpeg)

The second question was left out of the Pulse of Democracy report. Instead,
the report's Cuba chapter leads with the heading "Blame Attribution Is
Directed at the Cuban Regime, Not the U.S.," citing the 74% figure.

Julia Jordan, Vanderbilt's spokesperson, told Belly of the Beast and Drop Site
the findings should be interpreted together.

Asked why the second question was not included in the report, she said the
Cuba chapter presents only a "small number" of results and that the public
data "allow researchers and journalists to examine additional questions."

It's not clear that any did. Media outlets**** and foreign policy journals
covering the poll cited only the first question.

Polling experts questioned the survey's methodology and how the results were
presented.

"A question that forces a single choice and one that allows shared
responsibility captures different things," said Mariano Torcal, deputy
director of the Research and Expertise Center for Survey Methodology (RECSM)
in Barcelona, Spain. "Readers are better served by seeing both [questions] and
understanding how each was asked."

Stanford professor Jon Krosnick, who specializes in studying survey
methodology, found flaws in both questions--one failed to define the crisis;
the other steered people toward a narrow set of explanations.

"Honestly, I wouldn't put much stock in either one," he said.

## A Nationally Representative Poll?

The Pulse of Democracy report describes the poll as "a rare window into how
Cubans understand the country's current crisis, who they hold responsible, and
what they see as the country's most urgent priorities."

The report omitted a key detail disclosed in LAPOP's [technical
documentation](https://www.vanderbilt.edu/center-for-global-
democracy/data/?lp_download=2719#page=3): respondents were drawn from a pool
of CubaData users who had registered through the Apretaste app. The app can be
downloaded on Android devices, but iPhone users must use a VPN to access it;
Apple's app store geoblocks users physically located in Cuba to avoid
violating U.S. sanctions. Apretaste is not widely known on the island--Belly
of the Beast and Drop Site asked more than three dozen Cubans if they had
heard of it and only one said they had (although they had not downloaded or
used it).

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TwaX!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9d79be34-eee8-40c2-94cd-2901d9b6c671_942x660.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TwaX!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9d79be34-eee8-40c2-94cd-2901d9b6c671_942x660.png)Screenshots
of the Apretaste app.

The app offers a kitchen sink of features, including daily prayers and jokes,
a dating service, and news (most of the featured media outlets are openly
opposed to the Cuban government, and several are U.S.-government funded).

Apretaste also offers a chance to win cash prizes in raffles by participating
in surveys. We entered false information about our age, marital status, race,
and education level in the most recent survey--about the importance of pets in
everyday life. There was no process to verify our identity.

Vanderbilt spokesperson Julia Jordan said CubaData screened for bots or "heavy
multi-device usage" and its "communication and data transfer are protected by
advanced encryption." She did not respond to questions about how respondents'
age and residence were verified or whether duplicate submissions could be
identified.

In exchange for completing the survey, we received virtual credits usable for
raffle entries. Winnings accumulate in a separate dollar-denominated balance.
Apretaste says users can [claim their
prizes](https://apretaste.net/ayuda/fiestas) as mobile phone credit with
Cubacel, Cuba's state-owned mobile service, or as USDT, a cryptocurrency
pegged to the U.S. dollar, once they reach its minimum payout threshold.

The app displayed more than 100 users who had won raffles for participating in
the AmericasBarometer survey. Each user's profile and information--including
name, age, race, and city of residence--was visible.

Vanderbilt has touted the poll, which it[
says](https://www.vanderbilt.edu/center-for-global-
democracy/data/?lp_download=2719) collected responses from 1,095 adults living
in Cuba, as "[the first-ever nationally representative
study](https://www.vanderbilt.edu/cgd/press/pbs-news-hour-cites-
americasbarometer-data-in-interview-with-cuban-official/)" of Cuba.

The report itself contradicts this claim, acknowledging the survey was not
nationally representative because it was based on an online panel that skewed
younger, more urban, and more connected to the internet.

According to Jordan, "political and security restrictions" prevented
researchers from randomly selecting respondents from Cuba's population.

She did not respond to questions about why a poll that was not nationally
representative was promoted as if it were.

"The researchers can claim that they collected data from a specific number of
Cubans, but they should not claim that the sample is nationally
representative," said Krosnick. "Simply stating that there is no other way to
conduct a survey in Cuba is not an excuse for the use of misleading language
that cultivates the impression that the survey is more rigorous and valuable
than it is."

## What Cubans Think Other Cubans Think

One of the report's featured findings states that "opposition to U.S. military
intervention appears limited."

Unlike[ the other 72 questions in the poll](https://cdn.vanderbilt.edu/vu-
wpfsx/wp-content/uploads/sites/157/2026/09/ABCub2026-Cuba-
Questionnaire-V6.2.4.2-Spa-260616-W.pdf), which asked respondents their
opinion, this question asked people what they thought other Cubans' opinions
were.

Forty-three percent answered that they believed most Cubans would support an
intervention. No question asked whether the respondents themselves would
support an intervention.

According to Jordan, the question was framed in this way due to Cuba's
"politically sensitive environment…where respondents may be reluctant to
disclose their personal views on controversial political questions."

However, the survey asked other seemingly controversial questions directly,
such as whether respondents had confidence in Cuba's president and whether
they believed the country should be annexed by the United States.

Krosnick questioned the value of asking people what they think about what
other people think.

"Answers should not be viewed as correctly indicating how other people would
feel or as correctly indicating how the respondent would feel," he said.

Jordan agreed.

"The results should not be interpreted as a direct measure of personal support
for military intervention," she wrote in an email response. "Nor should we
assume that respondents can accurately predict how other Cubans would react."

Jordan declined to answer why this disclaimer was not included in the Pulse of
Democracy report or in any of Vanderbilt's promotional language.

## A Long History of Shaping Public Opinion in Cuba

Despite the questions surrounding the LAPOP poll, its finding that many Cubans
blame their government for the country's crisis will come as no surprise to
anyone who spends time on the island.

Cuba's economy has been in free fall for eight years as "maximum pressure"
sanctions have scared off foreign trade, investment, and credit while
decimating the state's ability to provide basic social services that were long
taken for granted. Since January, Trump's oil blockade and punishing secondary
sanctions are plunging the country into a crisis that UN experts have called a
"[silent Gaza](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/08/1168094)."

But sanctions are an abstract concept. On the ground in Cuba, people can't see
executive orders and Treasury Department regulations--only their effects.

Turning hardship into anger directed at the Cuban government was precisely
what State Department official Lester Mallory proposed in an April 1960[
memo](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1958-60v06/d499) that
argued for economic warfare on Cuba**** less than**** two years**** before the
embargo was imposed by John F. Kennedy.

Mallory called for denying Cuba money and supplies to drive down wages, cause
hunger, and desperation, and bring about the government's overthrow. "The only
foreseeable means of alienating internal support," Mallory wrote, was "through
disenchantment and disaffection based on economic dissatisfaction and
hardship."

U.S. efforts to destroy Cuba's economy, he wrote, should be "as adroit and
inconspicuous as possible."

Sixty-six years later, Mallory's strategy is in full display.

As the U.S. government systematically cuts Cuba off from the rest of the
world, it also discreetly funnels millions of dollars a year to organizations
whose mission is to convince people both on and off the island that the Cuban
government is solely to blame for the country's economic crisis.

The recipients of those funds include media outlets aimed at a Cuban audience,
such as Diario de Cuba,__ that report on the country without mentioning U.S.
sanctions or their impact.

One question the LAPOP poll did not ask: Where do Cubans receive news and
information about the causes of the crisis they are enduring?

If it had, the answers might have revealed that the same organizations and
individuals measuring public opinion in Cuba were also shaping it.
